description:
Astro Beat es un equipo multidisciplinario y virtual enfocado en diseñar una solución tecnológica para el monitoreo inteligente de la salud de los astronautas durante misiones espaciales.
Nuestro objetivo es desarrollar una herramienta que permita recopilar, analizar y visualizar signos vitales y métricas biométricas de forma clara, segura y accesible, ayudando a prevenir riesgos médicos y mejorar el bienestar de la tripulación en entornos de microgravedad.
summary: Astro Beat is an interactive onboard health-monitoring system designed for long-duration missions, where communication delays and the lack of emergency evacuation require greater crew autonomy. It addresses the challenge of monitoring astronaut health by integrating three complementary data sources: vital signs, self-reported symptoms, and activity tracking to support well-being through exercise, rest, relaxation, sleep, and cognitive health activities. Rather than relying solely on fixed terrestrial thresholds, AstroBeat compares measurements with each astronaut’s personal baseline, evaluates data quality and persistence, and identifies gradual or combined changes over time. It classifies the astronaut’s status as normal, attention, or critical, and provides clear alerts, step-by-step recommendations, and locally stored health records. This approach is important because health problems may develop progressively before becoming serious or critical. By helping astronauts recognize changes in their physical and cognitive health early, Astro Beat supports prevention and timely action without replacing clinical judgment.
details:
Project Overview

Astro Beat is a health-monitoring system designed for astronauts during long-duration missions. It is intended to support crew autonomy by collecting, interpreting, and presenting health information locally, even when communication with Earth is delayed or unavailable.

How the System Works

Astro Beat uses a three-layer architecture: data acquisition, local processing, and user interaction.

The proposed data-acquisition layer is based on a biocompatible hydrogel patch attached directly to the astronaut’s skin. is based on a biocompatible hydrogel patch attached directly to the astronaut’s skin. The patch would integrate multiple sensors to collect indicators associated with different physiological functions relevant to health evaluation:

  • Cardiovascular function: heart rate.
  • Respiratory function: blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂).
  • Brain and cognitive function: stress and sleep quality.
  • Metabolic function: body temperature.

After acquiring and digitizing the physiological signals, the patch would transmit the data to a compatible smartwatch through human-body communication. The smartwatch would act as a local receiving and processing device.

The system would also allow astronauts to manually report symptoms such as fatigue, dizziness, headache, difficulty concentrating, or thirst. Symptoms could be recorded together with their perceived intensity on a scale from 1 to 10. In addition, astronauts could log wellness-related activities, including exercise, nutrition, hydration, rest, relaxation, sleep, and activities that support cognitive well-being.

Local Processing and Decision Support

The processing layer organizes the information using timestamps, measurement conditions, data quality, device status, and synchronization status. It checks whether each measurement is complete, recent, and reliable before using it in the assessment.

Astro Beat compares new measurements with reference ranges, the astronaut’s personal baseline, and previous trends. It evaluates whether a change is isolated or persistent and whether it appears together with a reported symptom or another abnormal indicator. This allows the system to distinguish between a potentially meaningful change and an isolated or unreliable measurement.

Based on these criteria, Astro Beat classifies the astronaut’s status as normal, attention, or critical. The system provides an explanation for each alert and recommends a next action, such as repeating a measurement, resting, monitoring a symptom, completing an additional assessment, or contacting Mission Control.

User Interface

The user-interaction layer presents the processed information through a crew-oriented interface. The prototype includes a main health dashboard, detailed vital-sign screens with 24-hour, 7-day, and 30-day views, symptom check-ins, activity and wellness tracking, an alert center, emergency guidance, recommendations, and local history.

The interface displays the current value, trend, measurement quality, last update, alert priority, and recommended action. Health events are stored locally when communication is unavailable and placed in a synchronization queue for later transmission to Mission Control.

Technical Implementation

The current prototype was developed using HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript ES2020. We used a Ports and Adapters architecture to separate data sources, processing logic, and the graphical interface. This separation allows the system to operate with simulated and manually entered data while remaining open to future integration with real sensors.

The hydrogel patch, physical sensors, smartwatch receiver, and human-body communication channel are proposed hardware components and have not yet been integrated or validated. The current demonstration focuses on the software workflow and interface.

Creative Contribution

Astro Beat is not limited to displaying isolated vital-sign measurements. Its creative contribution is the combination of physiological data, self-reported symptoms, activity, and wellness information in a single decision-support workflow. The system evaluates changes over time, considers the astronaut’s individual baseline, identifies persistent or combined changes, and translates the results into understandable actions.

This approach also incorporates activities that support physical recovery, rest, relaxation, sleep, and cognitive well-being, recognizing that astronaut health includes both physical and cognitive dimensions.

It is designed to process information locally without requiring a continuous connection to Earth, while storing health events for synchronization with mission control once communication is restored.

Market Opportunity

Astro Beat is primarily envisioned as an early, low-cost way to explore this problem before the development of a complete flight-ready system.

The expected return is validated knowledge, a tested software workflow, documented mission scenarios, and a foundation for future health-monitoring technologies. If the results reveal that certain assumptions are incorrect, that information is also valuable because it prevents larger investments in an ineffective design.

Strong performance could position this as a B2B/B2G solution for space agencies, commercial space operators, aerospace-medicine centers, analog mission programs, and research institutions. These organizations require compact and reliable systems that can support crew health monitoring during missions with communication delays and limited access to medical resources.

The same software architecture could later be adapted for terrestrial environments where medical assistance is limited or delayed, including polar research stations, offshore platforms, military operations, mining sites, disaster-response teams, and remote healthcare programs.

Additional revenue could come from sensor and data-system integration, customization, technical support, and long-term maintenance. The hydrogel patch and communication hardware could initially be developed through partnerships with biosensor manufacturers rather than being produced directly by AstroBeat.

Intended Impact and Future Development

Astro Beat is intended to support earlier recognition of gradual physical or cognitive deterioration and enable timely action before a developing problem becomes a serious episode. It is designed to support astronauts and medical personnel by providing organized, interpretable, and locally available information.

Future development would include integrating real sensors, validating the hydrogel patch and communication channel, testing the system under movement and mission-analog conditions, refining alert thresholds, and evaluating usability, data security, reliability, and clinical interpretability. AstroBeat is intended to support medical decision-making, not diagnose conditions or replace professional medical judgment.
